Action Plan:
1. Book a face-to-face GP appointment within the next few days for chest examination and peak flow assessment; determine need for antibiotics and/or oral steroids based on findings.
2. Increase brown preventer inhaler (Clenil) to 4 puffs twice daily until reviewed.
3. Use blue inhaler (salbutamol) as needed, up to every 2–4 hours; frequent need indicates poor control—seek earlier review.
4. Safety-net: If breathing worsens or if frequent blue inhaler use is required without improvement, go to the Emergency Department (A&E) and do not wait for the GP appointment.
5. Verbal consent from patient has been obtained before using transcription software.

Subjective:
- Presenting complaint: 2–3 days of increased shortness of breath, wheeze, and cough; began during a run; now occurs with brisk walking; minimal relief from blue inhaler.
- Sputum: None reported.
- Asthma history:
  - Known asthma.
  - Last asthma attack 3–4 years ago.
  - No prior hospital admissions for asthma.
  - No history of oral steroids recalled.
  - Last asthma review approximately 2 years ago.
- Inhaler use:
  - Blue inhaler (salbutamol) used daily and as needed; patient has been using it in the morning/evening “to prevent” symptoms as well.
  - Preventer inhaler used twice daily; patient did not clearly state the name; clinician later referred to Clenil (brown inhaler).
- Peak flow: Patient agrees usual reading is about “380” when well; has not checked since symptom onset; performs peak flow only occasionally.
- Allergies: Hay fever; denies medication allergies.
- Family history: Brother with asthma; sister with eczema.
- Dermatologic: Patient suspects possible eczema; uses Cetraben and hydrocortisone (dose/route/frequency not documented). Patient initially mentioned “Bactroban,” then clarified Cetraben (conflict noted).

Objective:
- No vitals or physical examination performed (telehealth consultation).
- No investigations performed during this consult.

Assessment & Plan:

1. Shortness of breath/wheeze in known asthma:
   - Assessment or likely diagnosis: Mild asthma exacerbation.
   - Investigations planned: Face-to-face chest examination and peak flow measurement at upcoming visit; further testing as indicated by findings.
   - Treatment planned: Increase Clenil (brown inhaler) to 4 puffs twice daily; use salbutamol (blue inhaler) as needed up to every 2–4 hours; safety-net to attend Emergency Department (A&E) if worsening or needing frequent reliever.
   - Relevant referrals: Arrange GP face-to-face appointment within a few days.

2. Allergic rhinitis (hay fever):
   - Assessment or likely diagnosis: Allergic rhinitis.
   - Treatment planned: No changes discussed today.

3. Possible eczema:
   - Assessment or likely diagnosis: Possible eczema (patient-reported).
   - Treatment planned: Patient currently using hydrocortisone and Cetraben (dose/route/frequency not documented); no changes discussed today.

Quality checks:
- Missing expected elements: No vitals (including oxygen saturation), no objective respiratory exam, no detailed asthma control assessment, no trigger or infection review, no smoking status, no spacer use/inhaler technique review, no comprehensive medication list with doses/routes/frequencies, no written asthma action plan, no vaccination status.
- Internal conflicts: Medications—patient initially listed “Salbutamol, Flanel Bactroban and Hydrocortisone,” later clarified “Cetraben and Hydrocortisone”; preventer name not stated by patient, clinician referred to Clenil; baseline peak flow “about 380” suggested by clinician and agreed by patient—exact baseline uncertain.
- Transcript quality: Some unclear/inaudible segments and interruptions leading to ambiguity in medication names and dosing details.
